scenes.tts: Fill an excised lung with saline instead of air, and it takes far less pressure to inflate it to the same volume. The tissue is the same both times. In nineteen twenty-nine, Kurt von Neergaard compared an isolated pig lung filled with air and with a gum solution. The liquid removes the air-liquid surface that lines every alveolus. He concluded that surface tension, not tissue elasticity, accounts for most of the lung's recoil.
scenes.visual: A lung block, air-filled then liquid-filled, and two pressure-volume curves in this sketch: the liquid-filled curve far to the left of the air-filled one.

scenes.tts: So how hard is it to keep one alveolus open? Laplace's relation answers it for a single spherical air-liquid surface. The pressure equals two T divided by r. T is the surface tension, and r is the radius. Take a radius of one hundred micrometres and a tension of seventy millinewtons per metre, with no surfactant. These are illustrative values. The pressure is fourteen point three centimetres of water.
scenes.visual: One idealised alveolus sphere with a surface rim, radius r, tension arrows, and the equation filled in step by step to 14.3 cmH2O.

scenes.tts: Now halve the radius to fifty micrometres, at the same tension. The pressure doubles, to twenty-eight point six centimetres of water. Join the two alveoli to one airway. At equal tension, the small alveolus would empty into the large one. Surface tension makes the smaller space harder to hold open.
scenes.visual: Plot of P = 2T/r with markers at 100 and 50 micrometres, then two alveoli on one airway with a red arrow from small to large.

scenes.tts: Surfactant changes that. In the nineteen fifties, John Clements put films from rat, cat and dog lung extracts on a surface balance. A movable barrier compresses the film, and a thin plate hanging in the surface reports the tension. The tension depended on area. It fell from about forty-six to about ten dynes per centimetre as the film was compressed. The name surfactant came later.
scenes.visual: A trough with a film, a barrier that moves in and a hanging plate, beside a tension-against-area plot where the point falls from about 46 to about 10 dynes per cm.

scenes.tts: Give the alveoli a lining whose tension falls as the area falls. These values are illustrative, and the tension in the small alveolus is made up. At one hundred micrometres, with surfactant, tension is twenty millinewtons per metre. The pressure is four point one centimetres of water. At fifty micrometres, tension is five millinewtons per metre. The pressure is two point zero, below the large alveolus. The small one no longer empties.
scenes.visual: The same two alveoli: rims turn to surfactant colour, the old arrow and numbers are cleared, new tensions and pressures appear, 2.0 below 4.1.
scenes.caption: Give the alveoli a lining whose tension falls as the area falls. These values are illustrative, and the tension in the small alveolus is made up. At 100 micrometres, with surfactant, tension is 20 mN/m. The pressure is 4.1 cmH2O. At 50 micrometres, tension is 5 mN/m. The pressure is 2.0 cmH2O, below the large alveolus. The small one no longer empties.

scenes.tts: This emptying is a result of theory and of films studied in vitro. Whether a film prevents it depends on how steeply tension changes with area. Real alveoli are also tethered. Neighbours share walls, so one alveolus cannot shrink alone like a free bubble. Keep this rule. Surface tension makes small alveoli harder to hold open, and surfactant lowers tension most when the alveolus is small.
scenes.visual: Caveats as chips, a tethered four-block schematic with shared walls, then the rule.
